title: Why Git? Mental Model & Architecture
description: Understand the problems version control solves, how Git tracks snapshots instead of diffs, and the Three Trees architecture.

blocks.content:
## The Problem Version Control Solves

Before version control systems (VCS), tracking revisions meant saving files with chaotic names:
- `project_v1.py`
- `project_v2_final.py`
- `project_v2_final_REALLY_FINAL.py`
- `project_v2_final_REALLY_FINAL_sam_edits.zip`

This approach breaks instantly:
1. **No Concurrency**: Two developers modifying the same file overwrite each other's changes.
2. **No Accountability**: No record of who changed what, when, or why.
3. **No Safe Rollback**: Reverting to a known good state requires manually untangling changes.
4. **No Experimentation**: Trying a new feature risks breaking working production code.

## What is Git?

Git is a **Distributed Version Control System (DVCS)** created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds to manage the Linux kernel. Unlike centralized systems (like SVN or CVS) where history lives only on a single remote server, every developer cloning a Git repository receives a complete copy of the entire project history.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Centralized [Centralized VCS: SVN / CVS]
        ServerCentral["Central Server (History Lives Here)"]
        ClientA["Developer A (Working Copy Only)"]
        ClientB["Developer B (Working Copy Only)"]
        ServerCentral <--> ClientA
        ServerCentral <--> ClientB
    end

    subgraph Distributed [Distributed VCS: Git]
        RemoteRepo[("Remote Repo / GitHub")]
        Dev1[("Local Repo 1 (Full History)")]
        Dev2[("Local Repo 2 (Full History)")]
        RemoteRepo <--> Dev1
        RemoteRepo <--> Dev2
        Dev1 <-.-> Dev2
    end
```

If the server crashes or goes offline, any developer's local repository can restore the entire project history.

## Core Concept: Snapshots, Not Differences

Traditional VCS tools store information as a list of file-based changes (deltas):

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph DeltaVCS [Delta-Based VCS]
        D1["Version 1: File A, File B, File C"]
        D2["Version 2: Diff A1, Diff C1"]
        D3["Version 3: Diff C2"]
        D1 --> D2 --> D3
    end
```

Git does not store diffs. Git thinks of its data as a **stream of snapshots**. Every time you commit, Git takes a picture of what all your files look like at that exact moment, and stores a reference to that snapshot. If a file has not changed, Git does not store the file again; it simply links to the previous identical copy.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph SnapshotVCS [Git Snapshot Model]
        S1["Commit 1\nFile A1 | File B1 | File C1"]
        S2["Commit 2\nFile A2 | File B1 (link) | File C2"]
        S3["Commit 3\nFile A2 (link) | File B1 (link) | File C3"]
        S1 --> S2 --> S3
    end
```

## The Three Trees of Git

Git manages your files across three separate areas:

1. **Working Directory (Working Tree)**: The actual files on your filesystem that you open, edit, and run in your editor.
2. **Staging Area (Index)**: A staging preview of the exact files and modifications that will go into your next commit.
3. **Git Directory (Repository / HEAD)**: The permanent database (`.git` folder) where Git stores compressed snapshots and commit history.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Working Directory\n(Sandbox / Editing)"] -->|"git add"| B["Staging Area / Index\n(Prepared Snapshot)"]
    B -->|"git commit"| C["Git Repository\n(Permanent History / HEAD)"]
    C -->|"git checkout / restore"| A
```

blocks.question: How does Git store file history compared to older delta-based version control systems?
options: Git stores line-by-line differences (deltas) between consecutive versions
Git stores a complete snapshot of the project state, reusing links for unchanged files
Git only saves files that contain syntax errors
Git uploads raw file copies to a single central server on every file save
blocks.explanation: Git treats data as a sequence of full project snapshots. Unchanged files are referenced via SHA pointers to existing stored objects rather than re-saving duplicate contents.

blocks.question: Which area in Git holds the staged changes that are lined up for the next commit?
blocks.explanation: The Staging Area (or Index) holds the exact set of changes you have prepared via 'git add' to be committed in the next 'git commit' snapshot.
